PROCEDURE DETAILS:
Pre-procedure
COMPARISON: None
Informed consent for the procedure was obtained and time-out was performed prior to the procedure.
Preparation (MIPS): The site was prepared and draped using all elements of maximal sterile barrier
technique including sterile gloves, sterile gown, cap, mask, large sterile sheet, sterile ultrasound
probe cover, hand hygiene and cutaneous antisepsis
with povidone-iodine.

Anesthesia/Sedation
Level of anesthesia/sedation: No sedation
Anesthesia/sedation administered by: Not applicable
Total intra-service sedation time: 30 minutes.
Access

access. Real time ultrasound was used to visualize needle entry into the liver and a permanent image was
stored.
Access side: Right
Access ultrasound findings: No focal hepatic mass.
Access technique: 20-gauge coaxial biopsy needle
TECHNIQUE:
The patient was positioned supine. The skin of the abdomen overlying the liver was prepped and draped in
the usual sterile fashion. After local anesthesia with 8 mL 2% lidocaine without epinephrine and using
real-time ultrasound guidance, the needle
was advanced percutaneously into the liver. The specimen(s) were obtained.
Closure
The needle was removed and hemostasis was achieved with manual compression. Sterile dressing(s) applied.

Additional description of procedure: None
Additional findings: None

Kleinman, Michael S, DO 12/1/2021 5:31 PM
EMG & NCV Findings:
Motor conduction studies of the left peroneal nerve recording
extensor digitorum brevis demonstrated a severely reduced (nearly
absent) response amplitude with stimulation at the ankle. The
distal latency is severely prolonged though this is not
considered to be technically accurate given how low the response
amplitude is.
Motor conduction studies of the left peroneal nerve recording
tibialis anterior demonstrates a normal distal latency,
moderately reduced response amplitudes and normal conduction
velocity across the fibular head.
Motor conduction studies of the left tibial nerve demonstrated a
moderately prolonged distal latency, severely reduced response
amplitudes and mildly slowed conduction velocity. F-wave minimum
latency was moderately prolonged.
Motor conduction studies of the right peroneal nerve recording
extensor digitorum brevis demonstrated a severely reduced (nearly
absent) response amplitude with stimulation at the ankle.
Motor conduction studies of the right tibial nerve with
stimulation at the ankle demonstrated a mildly prolonged distal
latency and severely reduced response amplitude.
Motor conduction studies of the left ulnar nerve were normal,
including F-wave minimal latency.
The left sural sensory response was absent. Sensory conduction
study of the right sural nerve demonstrated a severely reduced
response amplitude and moderately slowed conduction velocity.
Sensory conduction study of the left radial nerve was normal.
Concentric needle electromyography (EMG) was performed in
selected muscles representing the left L4-S1 myotomes. Mild
active denervation with moderate chronic reinnervation and mildly
reduced recruitment was seen in tibialis anterior. Severe
chronic reinnervation with mildly reduced recruitment was seen in
extensor hallucis longus. Mild chronic reinnervation was seen in
medial gastrocnemius. Vastus lateralis was normal.
Impression:
Abnormal study. The electrophysiologic data is consistent with a
severe axonal generalized sensorimotor polyneuropathy.

EXAM: ULTRASOUND-GUIDED PERCUTANEOUS RANDOM CORE LIVER BIOPSY
INDICATION: Ultrasound-guided liver biopsy requested. Reactive arthritis. Elevated ALT, AST. Evaluate
for hemochromatosis with quantitative iron evaluation as well.
COMPARISON: Ultrasound 12/23/14.
FINDINGS: Identification and procedure time out were performed. Signed informed consent was obtained.
The biopsy was performed by Dr. Winn with Dr. Brian Alan Perry.
An oblique right intercostal approach was selected. Realtime ultrasound guidance was used throughout the
procedure. Standard sterile preparation and technique were employed. Local anesthesia was obtained with
infusion of 1% lidocaine solution. A
biopsy was performed with coaxial technique with the need for multiple core specimens for the diagnostic
testing requested, per discussion with the Pathology department prior to the procedure. With realtime
ultrasound guidance, a 17-gauge introducer
needle was placed into the right lobe of the liver. A biopsy was performed through that with an 18-gauge
spring loaded automatic core biopsy needle. Two separate 2 cm long cores were obtained. These were
placed together in a single container of
formalin and submitted for histopathologic evaluation and quantitative iron evaluation. The biopsy
needle was removed and stylet was placed within the coaxial needle. After approximately 3 minutes the
stylet was removed and revealed no bleeding through
the coaxial needle. The coaxial needle was then removed. Postbiopsy imaging showed no evidence of
hemorrhage or immediate perihepatic hematoma.
The site was cleansed and a band-aid was applied. The patient was placed in right lateral decubitus
recumbency and brought to the radiology nursing area for postbiopsy observation with orders placed in the
electronic medical record. Specimen was
submitted for diagnostic testing as ordered.
IMPRESSION: Ultrasound-guided percutaneous random core liver biopsy performed. Details above.

Kleinman, Michael S, DO 12/1/2021 5:31 PM
EMG & NCV Findings:
Motor conduction studies of the left peroneal nerve recording
extensor digitorum brevis demonstrated a severely reduced (nearly
absent) response amplitude with stimulation at the ankle. The
distal latency is severely prolonged though this is not
considered to be technically accurate given how low the response
amplitude is.
Motor conduction studies of the left peroneal nerve recording
tibialis anterior demonstrates a normal distal latency,
moderately reduced response amplitudes and normal conduction
velocity across the fibular head.
Motor conduction studies of the left tibial nerve demonstrated a
moderately prolonged distal latency, severely reduced response
amplitudes and mildly slowed conduction velocity. F-wave minimum
latency was moderately prolonged.
Motor conduction studies of the right peroneal nerve recording
extensor digitorum brevis demonstrated a severely reduced (nearly
absent) response amplitude with stimulation at the ankle.
Motor conduction studies of the right tibial nerve with
stimulation at the ankle demonstrated a mildly prolonged distal
latency and severely reduced response amplitude.
Motor conduction studies of the left ulnar nerve were normal,
including F-wave minimal latency.
The left sural sensory response was absent. Sensory conduction
study of the right sural nerve demonstrated a severely reduced
response amplitude and moderately slowed conduction velocity.
Sensory conduction study of the left radial nerve was normal.
Concentric needle electromyography (EMG) was performed in
selected muscles representing the left L4-S1 myotomes. Mild
active denervation with moderate chronic reinnervation and mildly
reduced recruitment was seen in tibialis anterior. Severe
chronic reinnervation with mildly reduced recruitment was seen in
extensor hallucis longus. Mild chronic reinnervation was seen in
medial gastrocnemius. Vastus lateralis was normal.
Impression:
Abnormal study. The electrophysiologic data is consistent with a
severe axonal generalized sensorimotor polyneuropathy.

EXAM: ULTRASOUND-GUIDED PERCUTANEOUS RANDOM CORE LIVER BIOPSY
INDICATION: Ultrasound-guided liver biopsy requested. Reactive arthritis. Elevated ALT, AST. Evaluate
for hemochromatosis with quantitative iron evaluation as well.
COMPARISON: Ultrasound 12/23/14.
FINDINGS: Identification and procedure time out were performed. Signed informed consent was obtained.
The biopsy was performed by Dr. Winn with Dr. Brian Alan Perry.
An oblique right intercostal approach was selected. Realtime ultrasound guidance was used throughout the
procedure. Standard sterile preparation and technique were employed. Local anesthesia was obtained with
infusion of 1% lidocaine solution. A
biopsy was performed with coaxial technique with the need for multiple core specimens for the diagnostic
testing requested, per discussion with the Pathology department prior to the procedure. With realtime
ultrasound guidance, a 17-gauge introducer
needle was placed into the right lobe of the liver. A biopsy was performed through that with an 18-gauge
spring loaded automatic core biopsy needle. Two separate 2 cm long cores were obtained. These were
placed together in a single container of
formalin and submitted for histopathologic evaluation and quantitative iron evaluation. The biopsy
needle was removed and stylet was placed within the coaxial needle. After approximately 3 minutes the
stylet was removed and revealed no bleeding through
the coaxial needle. The coaxial needle was then removed. Postbiopsy imaging showed no evidence of
hemorrhage or immediate perihepatic hematoma.
The site was cleansed and a band-aid was applied. The patient was placed in right lateral decubitus
recumbency and brought to the radiology nursing area for postbiopsy observation with orders placed in the
electronic medical record. Specimen was
submitted for diagnostic testing as ordered.
IMPRESSION: Ultrasound-guided percutaneous random core liver biopsy performed. Details above.

causes of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. The Kleiner activity score
and fibrosis are provided. A reticulin stain highlights non-neoplastic
hepatic plate architecture with focal areas of collapse. An iron stain
is focally positive within the Kupffer cells. There is no hepatocyte or
bile duct accumulation of iron. The iron does not appear increased
significantly. Serologic iron testing may be influenced by the
steatohepatitis identified. No prominent intracytoplasmic globules are
identified on PAS/PAS-D stains. A trichrome stain shows a pattern of
fibrosis limited to the zone 3.

department for further evaluation. Patient denies any vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, tremors, difficulty with coordination.

**Assessment and Plan**:
William B Seretta is a 39 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to mania and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (
e.g. having had several million dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without
collateral information this is hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow,
discuss with parents for more comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention
which have persisted despite treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined
type given history of inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also
consider diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Regarding the possibility of antidepressant treatment, William has a history of one prolonged manic episode that lasted for weeks. I
am skeptical that this was an entirely substance induced episode given that his mania continued in the absence of substance use
and with concurrent medication treatment. I am concerned about the possibility of antidepressant treatment given the evidence
that antidepressants disrupt the course of bipolar disorder meaning that it could lead to mania or worsening depression.
Additionally, there is the phenomenon of antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria in patients with a bipolar spectrum
disorder. My preference at this time is to continue lamotrigine titration which is indicated for bipolar depression. Additionally,
lithium is also indicated for bipolar depression.
Treatment progress: William has had periods of improved depression, but largely struggles with low mood and motivation and
anxiety. Working with Charles Morris in therapy has been very beneficial. Impairment in occupational functioning- has not been
working due to symptoms. Started on guanfacine for anxiety/adhd.
**6/25/26: **reports identifying pattern where his mood cycles from feeling more or less motivated and down. Has been working in
therapy to accept these changes and modify behaviors and expectations accordingly. Making positive changes to exercise and self

care. Encouraged to obtain repeat lithium level due to recent decrease in dose. Endorses difficulty with relaxation and ongoing
anxiety, along with chronic struggles wit executive function. Discuss starting guanfacine for anxiety and adhd. Encouraged using
hydroxyzine sparingly with this medication addition.

William B Seretta is a 39 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to mania and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of De
pakote and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several
million dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information
this is hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for
more comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted
despite treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Regarding the possibility of antidepressant treatment, William has a history of one prolonged manic episode that lasted for weeks. I
am skeptical that this was an entirely substance induced episode given that his mania continued in the absence of substance use
and with concurrent medication treatment. I am concerned about the possibility of antidepressant treatment given the evidence
that antidepressants disrupt the course of bipolar disorder meaning that it could lead to mania or worsening depression.
Additionally, there is the phenomenon of antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria in patients with a bipolar spectrum
disorder. My preference at this time is to continue lamotrigine titration which is indicated for bipolar depression. Additionally,
lithium is also indicated for bipolar depression.
Treatment progress: William has had periods of improved depression, but largely struggles with low mood and motivation and
anxiety. Working with Charles Morris in therapy has been very beneficial. Impairment in occupational functioning- has not been
working due to symptoms.

William B Seretta is a 38 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to mania and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully asc
ertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more comprehensive
history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite treatment of his
underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of inattention, hyperactivity,
and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis of generalized anxiety
disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Regarding the possibility of antidepressant treatment, William has a history of one prolonged manic episode that lasted for weeks. I
am skeptical that this was an entirely substance induced episode given that his mania continued in the absence of substance use
and with concurrent medication treatment. I am concerned about the possibility of antidepressant treatment given the evidence

that antidepressants disrupt the course of bipolar disorder meaning that it could lead to mania or worsening depression.
Additionally, there is the phenomenon of antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria in patients with a bipolar spectrum
disorder. My preference at this time is to continue lamotrigine titration which is indicated for bipolar depression. Additionally,
lithium is also indicated for bipolar depression.

William B Seretta is a 38 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to mania and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, an
d should patient allow, discuss with parents for more comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of
anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms
include ADHD, combined type given history of inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's
daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor
concentration and fatigue.
Regarding the possibility of antidepressant treatment, William has a history of one prolonged manic episode that lasted for weeks. I
am skeptical that this was an entirely substance induced episode given that his mania continued in the absence of substance use
and with concurrent medication treatment. I am concerned about the possibility of antidepressant treatment given the evidence
that antidepressants disrupt the course of bipolar disorder meaning that it could lead to mania or worsening depression.
Additionally, there is the phenomenon of antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria in patients with a bipolar spectrum
disorder. My preference at this time is to continue lamotrigine titration which is indicated for bipolar depression. Additionally,

lithium is also indicated for bipolar depression.

William B Seretta is a 38 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents
for more comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted
despite treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Regarding the possibility of antidepressant treatment, William has a history of one prolonged manic episode that lasted for weeks. I
am skeptical that this was an entirely substance induced episode given that his mania continued in the absence of substance use
and with concurrent medication treatment. I am concerned about the possibility of antidepressant treatment given the evidence
that antidepressants disrupt the course of bipolar disorder meaning that it could lead to mania or worsening depression.
Additionally, there is the phenomenon of antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria in patients with a bipolar spectrum
disorder. My preference at this time is to continue lamotrigine titration which is indicated for bipolar depression. Additionally,
lithium is also indicated for bipolar depression.

**12/11/25: **William reports that overall his mood has been stable for the last several months. He continues to progress towards
goals in therapy. Notes that anxiety and restlessness continues to be more present. Has PRN hydroxyzine that is partially effective,
advised to focus on coping skills and behavioral strategies as well as incrasing hydroxyzine dose to up to 50mg. Declined referral to
vocational services at this time, but open to considering in future.

William B Seretta is a 38 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Regarding the possibility of antidepressant treatment, William has a history of one prolonged manic episode that lasted for weeks. I

am skeptical that this was an entirely substance induced episode given that his mania continued in the absence of substance use
and with concurrent medication treatment. I am concerned about the possibility of antidepressant treatment given the evidence
that antidepressants disrupt the course of bipolar disorder meaning that it could lead to mania or worsening depression.
Additionally, there is the phenomenon of antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria in patients with a bipolar spectrum
disorder. My preference at this time is to continue lamotrigine titration which is indicated for bipolar depression. Additionally,
lithium is also indicated for bipolar depression.
**9/11/25: **William reports that overall his mood has been stable for the last several months. He continues to progress towards
goals in therapy. Notes that anxiety has now come to the forefront, in the form of ruminative thinking. He recently stopped
drinking alcohol which has overall been a positive change. We discuss ways to manage anxiety through ongoing work w/ therapy
and utilization of coping skills such as mindfulness. Additionally, he would like to try hydroxyzine PRN for more support. Discussed
r/b/se. Encouraged to obtain monitoring labs for lithium (CMP, TSH, and Li Level).

William B Seretta is a 38 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite

treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Regarding the possibility of antidepressant treatment, William has a history of one prolonged manic episode that lasted for weeks. I
am skeptical that this was an entirely substance induced episode given that his mania continued in the absence of substance use
and with concurrent medication treatment. I am concerned about the possibility of antidepressant treatment given the evidence
that antidepressants disrupt the course of bipolar disorder meaning that it could lead to mania or worsening depression.
Additionally, there is the phenomenon of antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria in patients with a bipolar spectrum
disorder. My preference at this time is to continue lamotrigine titration which is indicated for bipolar depression. Additionally,
lithium is also indicated for bipolar depression.
Today, William is quite perseverative on the role of anxiety in his life. He expresses feeling frustrated that has not been addressed
previously and that he has not realized the role is playing. I shared my belief that he has been showing slow improvements in
energy and motivation that I think a representative of improvement in his depression. With these changes, his anxiety has become
more apparent. We started working on CBT for anxiety including identifying manageable goals and how core beliefs about himself
get in the way of accomplishing these goals.

William B Seretta is a 37 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Regarding the possibility of antidepressant treatment, William has a history of one prolonged manic episode that lasted for weeks. I
am skeptical that this was an entirely substance induced episode given that his mania continued in the absence of substance use
and with concurrent medication treatment. I am concerned about the possibility of antidepressant treatment given the evidence
that antidepressants disrupt the course of bipolar disorder meaning that it could lead to mania or worsening depression.
Additionally, there is the phenomenon of antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria in patients with a bipolar spectrum
disorder. My preference at this time is to continue lamotrigine titration which is indicated for bipolar depression. Additionally,
lithium is also indicated for bipolar depression.
Today, William continues to make progress on accomplishing small goals with sustained improvement in his mood since titration of
lamotrigine. Was able to taper clonazepam without issue and we will plan to discontinue today. Regarding polypharmacy, we did
discuss my concerns about Adderall use. As William is skeptical of his bipolar diagnosis, he does not believe that the risk of bipolar
depression or mania applies to him. We will continue to work on using behavioral activation to accomplish tasks.

dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Today, William endorses sustained improvement in his sleep schedule leading to increase in motivation and activity level as well as
trying to improve his appetite. As a result, he reports finding enjoyment in activities for the first time in some time. This is in the
setting of relatively recent lamotrigine initiation as well as discussion about the limits of medication efficacy.
Regarding the possibility of antidepressant treatment, William has a history of one prolonged manic episode that lasted for weeks. I
am skeptical that this was an entirely substance induced episode given that his mania continued in the absence of substance use
and with concurrent medication treatment. I am concerned about the possibility of antidepressant treatment given the evidence
that antidepressants disrupt the course of bipolar disorder meaning that it could lead to mania or worsening depression.
Additionally, there is the phenomenon of antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria in patients with a bipolar spectrum
disorder. My preference at this time is to continue lamotrigine titration which is indicated for bipolar depression. Additionally,
lithium is also indicated for bipolar depression.

William B Seretta is a 37 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Today, William endorses improvement in his sleep schedule leading to increase in motivation and activity level as well as trying to
improve his appetite. As a result, he reports finding enjoyment in activities for the first time in some time. This is in the setting of
relatively recent lamotrigine initiation as well as discussion about the limits of medication efficacy.
Regarding the possibility of antidepressant treatment, William has a history of one prolonged manic episode that lasted for weeks. I
am skeptical that this was an entirely substance induced episode given that his mania continued in the absence of substance use
and with concurrent medication treatment. I am concerned about the possibility of antidepressant treatment given the evidence
that antidepressants disrupt the course of bipolar disorder meaning that it could lead to mania or worsening depression.
Additionally, there is the phenomenon of antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria in patients with a bipolar spectrum
disorder. My preference at this time is to continue lamotrigine titration which is indicated for bipolar depression. Additionally,
lithium is also indicated for bipolar depression.

William B Seretta is a 37 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is

hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Today, William continues to endorse significant difficulties with sleep, energy level, and mood. William has presented with this
persistent dysphoria for sometime and identifies difficulties in self-esteem and motivation as contributing. I also wonder about the
role of persistent cannabis and stimulant use. As William himself discusses, improvements in sleep hygiene such as spending more
time out of bed and exercising would likely be more therapeutic than further pharmacotherapy given his habits.
Regarding the possibility of antidepressant treatment, William has a history of one prolonged manic episode that lasted for weeks. I
am skeptical that this was an entirely substance induced episode given that his mania continued in the absence of substance use
and with concurrent medication treatment. I am concerned about the possibility of antidepressant treatment given the evidence
that antidepressants disrupt the course of bipolar disorder meaning that it could lead to mania or worsening depression.
Additionally, there is the phenomenon of antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria in patients with a bipolar spectrum
disorder. My preference at this time is to continue lamotrigine titration which is indicated for bipolar depression. Additionally,
lithium is also indicated for bipolar depression.

William B Seretta is a 37 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Today, William continues to endorse significant difficulties with sleep, energy level, and mood. William has presented with this
persistent dysphoria for sometime and identifies difficulties in self-esteem and motivation as contributing. I also wonder about the
role of persistent cannabis and stimulant use. As William himself discusses, improvements in sleep hygiene such as spending more

time out of bed and exercising would likely be more therapeutic than further pharmacotherapy given his habits.
Regarding the possibility of antidepressant treatment, William has a history of one prolonged manic episode that lasted for weeks. I
am skeptical that this was an entirely substance induced episode given that his mania continued in the absence of substance use
and with concurrent medication treatment. I am concerned about the possibility of antidepressant treatment given the evidence
that antidepressants disrupt the course of bipolar disorder meaning that it could lead to mania or worsening depression.
Additionally, there is the phenomenon of antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria in patients with a bipolar spectrum
disorder. My preference at this time is to continue lamotrigine titration which is indicated for bipolar depression. Additionally,
lithium is also indicated for bipolar depression.

William B Seretta is a 37 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Today, William continues to endorse significant difficulties with sleep, energy level,and mood. William has presented with this
persistent dysphoria for sometime and identifies difficulties in self-esteem and motivation as contributing. I also wonder about the
role of persistent cannabis and stimulant use. It is reasonable to trial lamotrigine for bipolar depression and is more favorable
option than a second generation antipsychotic given William's goal of weight loss. As William himself discusses, improvements in
sleep hygiene such as spending more time out of bed and exercising would likely be more therapeutic than further
pharmacotherapy given his habits.

**HPI:** William B Seretta is a 37 y.o. male with a history of bipolar disorder, ADHD, and polysubstance use disorder (stimulants,

-Endorses feeling more tired recently. We discussed lithium level and other lab results including elevated liver enzymes, however
they continue to trend down. Followed by Portland Gastro for this. Discussed elevated triglycerides and cholesterol. William
endorses that he has a "sedentary lifestyle and poor diet". Also endorses a family history of high cholesterol. We discussed the
possible contribution of quetiapine.
-William states that reducing quetiapine from 200 to 100 mg nightly after our last visit resulted in a number of side effects
including poor sleep, headache, reduced appetite, and nausea. This was surprising as he did not have any side effects when
reducing quetiapine from 400 to 200 mg. After a few days, the symptoms resolved. He wants to continue decreasing and then
discontinue quetiapine as "I do not think it is doing anything good for me". We discuss slowly tapering quetiapine by 25 mg every
week.
-States that sleep has been "consistent". He has noticed an increase in the intensity of his dreams following decrease in quetiapine
dose. States "I am kind of sick of it" as his dreams are more interesting then being awake.
-Continues to work with Charles on structure, having a reason to get up in the morning, and increasing motivation. Continues to
feel that therapy is very beneficial for him. States that most of his structuring a day is around doctors appointments and he "does
not do much for fun". States that his days "blur together" and "feel the same". "I need to do something else", and discusses going
to the gym and going back to work. Endorses the underlying issue as difficulty initiating things and feels that things get easier
once he starts them. Reports that he "works himself up beforehand".
-We discussed staying at the current lithium dose to decrease long term adverse effects. Discussed the possibility of augmenting
with lithium. Joint decision making to discuss this following discontinuation of quetiapine.

William B Seretta is a 37 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Today, William continues to struggle with symptoms of depression prominently anhedonia and fatigue. He is attempting to employ
behavioral interventions to increase his motivation and ability to do the things that he wants to do. This has been difficult as this is
a long-term pattern for him. Unfortunately, William experienced a discontinuation syndrome when reducing Seroquel. We will
slowly taper to attempt to avoid this. Following discontinuation of Seroquel, we will continue to explore possible augmentation
agents for lithium to treat bipolar depression.

William B Seretta is a 37 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Recent visits:
5-9/2022: Persistent depression/fatigue with no mania or psychosis. Altered medication admin timing of Depakote and gabapentin
without significant improvement
9/2022-5/2023: Tapered Haldol d/t possible contribution to bipolar depression. No recurrence of psychotic symptoms.
5/10/23: Ongoing depression and persistent sedation. Will complete Haldol taper in upcoming weeks. Will augment Depakote with
L-methylfolate given some evidence in bipolar depression and possible interruption of folate pathway with valproate.
8/4/23: Ongoing depression, requesting an SSRI.
9/5/23: Ongoing depression, starting escitalopram.
10/4/23: Ongoing depression, despite starting escitalopram 3 weeks prior. Difficulty falling asleep, even taking clonazepam nightly.
11/1/23: Ongoing depression, difficulty falling asleep, then sleeping more than 12 hours, and anxiety. Increased impulsivity, with
return to gambling. Given minimal effect and concern for activation, decreased escitalopram. Also decreasing clonazepam.
11/20/23: Worsening anxiety since decreasing clonazepam. Low mood and difficulty falling asleep, then sleeping excessively. Plan
to start quetiapine, taper off of escitalopram. Elevated LFTs noted, plan to recheck in several weeks.
1/5/24: Reports improved sleep and anxiety since star
ting quetiapine. Discontinuing Depakote due to LFTs.
2/2/24: Ongoing low mood and motivation. Able to fall asleep, but difficulty getting out of bed. Patient feels this is due to lack of
structure to his days rather than morning drowsiness. Discussed sleep hygiene and adding structure. Elected to taper gabapentin
due to lack of perceived benefit. Requesting an antidepressant.
3/1/24: William reports ongoing low mood, low motivation, and excessive sleep. He continues to spend much of his waking hours
lying in bed, though he acknowledges that inactivity causes his joint pain to worsen. His anxiety has increased, which he attributes
to tapering gabapentin. Dr. Abernathy's records were useful in clarifying her diagnostic impressions and his past medication history.
After reviewing risks and benefits of starting lithium to target mood, William verbally consents. He is being followed by Portland
Gastro for transaminitis and is getting labs drawn weekly, so will be able to have lithium monitoring labs drawn as well.
6/17/24: Mood appears stable on current medication regimen. Advised patient that next provider might not feel comfortable with
prescribing a benzodiazapine with concurrent adderall script. Will continue for now given patient is stable and I am not planning

on follow-up with him. PCP currently prescribes adderall. Will continue current medications.

William B Seretta is a 37 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.

without significant improvement

William B Seretta is a 36 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Recent visits:
5-9/2022: Persistent depression/fatigue with no mania or psychosis. Altered medication admin timing of Depakote and gabapentin
without significant improvement
9/2022-5/2023: Tapered Haldol d/t possible contribution to bipolar depression. No recurrence of psychotic symptoms.
5/10/23: Ongoing depression and persistent sedation. Will complete Haldol taper in upcoming weeks. Will augment Depakote with
L-methylfolate given some evidence in bipolar depression and possible interruption of folate pathway with valproate.
8/4/23: Ongoing depression, requesting an SSRI.
9/5/23: Ongoing depression, starting escitalopram.
10/4/23: Ongoing depression, despite starting escitalopram 3 weeks prior. Difficulty falling asleep, even taking clonazepam nightly.

return to gambling. Given minimal effect and concern for activation, decreased escitalopram. Also decreasing clonazepam.
11/20/23: Worsening anxiety since decreasing clonazepam. Low mood and difficulty falling asleep, then sleeping excessively. Plan
to start quetiapine, taper off of escitalopram. Elevated LFTs noted, plan to recheck in several weeks.
1/5/24: Reports improved sleep and anxiety since starting quetiapine. Discontinuing Depakote due to LFTs.

structure to his days rather than morning drowsiness. Discussed sleep hygiene and adding structure. Elected to taper gabapentin
due to lack of perceived benefit. Requesting an antidepressant.
3/1/24: Ongoing low mood, low motivation, and excessive sleep. Started on lithium. Anxiety has increased, which he attributes to
tapering gabapentin.

The needle was removed and hemostasis was achieved with manual compression. Sterile dressing(s) applied.

William B Seretta is a 36 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Recent visits:
5-9/2022: Persistent depression/fatigue with no mania or psychosis. Altered medication admin timing of Depakote and gabapentin
without significant improvement
9/2022-5/2023: Tapered Haldol d/t possible contribution to bipolar depression. No recurrence of psychotic symptoms.
5/10/23: Ongoing depression and persistent sedation. Will complete Haldol taper in upcoming weeks. Will augment Depakote with
L-methylfolate given some evidence in bipolar depression and possible interruption of folate pathway with valproate.
8/4/23: Ongoing depression, requesting an SSRI.
9/5/23: Ongoing depression, starting escitalopram.
10/4/23: Ongoing depression, despite starting escitalopram 3 weeks prior. Difficulty falling asleep, even taking clonazepam nightly.
11/1/23: Ongoing depression, difficulty falling asleep, then sleeping more than 12 hours, and anxiety. Increased impulsivity, with
return to gambling. Given minimal effect and concern for activation, decreased escitalopram. Also decreasing clonazepam.
11/20/23: Worsening anxiety since decreasing clonazepam. Low mood and difficulty falling asleep, then sleeping excessively. Plan
to start quetiapine, taper off of escitalopram. Elevated LFTs noted, plan to recheck in several weeks.
1/5/24: Reports improved sleep and anxiety since starting quetiapine. Discontinuing Depakote due to LFTs.
2/2/24: Ongoing low mood and motivation. Able to fall asleep, but difficulty getting out of bed. Patient feels this is due to lack of
structure to his days rather than morning drowsiness. Discussed sleep hygiene and adding structure. Elected to taper gabapentin
due to lack of perceived benefit. Requesting an antidepressant.
Today, William reports ongoing low mood, low motivation, and excessive sleep. He continues to spend much of his waking hours
lying in bed, though he acknowledges that inactivity causes his joint pain to worsen. His anxiety has increased, which he attributes
to tapering gabapentin. Dr. Abernathy's records were useful in clarifying her diagnostic impressions and his past medication history.

g lithium to target mood, William verbally consents. He is being followed by Portland Gastro for transaminitis and is getting labs

William B Seretta is a 36 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic medications.
Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin, which is currently
used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be continued for the time
being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider initiation of alpha agonist
medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating mania/psychosis than
stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and physician will be crucial in
providing effective care for the patient.

William B Seretta is a 36 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime
hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic medications.
Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin, which is currently
used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be continued for the time
being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider initiation of alpha agonist
medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating mania/psychosis than
stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and physician will be crucial in
providing effective care for the patient.

without significant improvement
9/2022-5/2023: Tapered Haldol d/t possible contribution to bipolar depression. No recurrence of psychotic symptoms.

L-methylfolate given some evidence in bipolar depression and possible interruption of folate pathway with valproate.
8/4/23: Ongoing depression, requesting an SSRI.
9/5/23: Ongoing depression, starting escitalopram.
10/4/23: Ongoing depression, despite starting escitalopram 3 weeks prior. Difficulty falling asleep, even taking clonazepam nightly.

11/20/23: Worsening anxiety since decreasing clonazepam. Low mood and difficulty falling asleep, then sleeping excessively. Plan

William B Seretta is a 36 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.

Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic medications.
Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin, which is currently
used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be continued for the time
being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider initiation of alpha agonist
medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating mania/psychosis than
stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and physician will be crucial in
providing effective care for the patient.

William B Seretta is a 36 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic medications.
Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin, which is currently
used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be continued for the time
being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider initiation of alpha agonist
medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating mania/psychosis than
stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and physician will be crucial in
providing effective care for the patient.

William B Seretta is a 36 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic
medications. Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin,
which is currently used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be
continued for the time being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider
initiation of alpha agonist medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating
mania/psychosis than stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and
physician will be crucial in providing effective care for the patient.

William B Seretta is a 36 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears eut
hymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote and Haldol. He does report some historical
elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million dollars, having millions of followers on
Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with
former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more comprehensive history. Primary complaints
on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite treatment of his underlying mood disorder.

Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this
is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of
generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic
medications. Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin,
which is currently used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be
continued for the time being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider
initiation of alpha agonist medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating
mania/psychosis than stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and
physician will be crucial in providing effective care for the patient.

5-9/2022: Persistent depression/fatigue with no mania or psychosis. Altered medication admin timing of Depakote and gabapentin
without significant improvement
9/2022-5/2023: Tapered Haldol d/t possible contribution to bipolar depression. No recurrence of psychotic symptoms.
5/10/23: Ongoing depression and persistent sedation. Will complete Haldol taper in upcoming weeks. Will augment Depakote with
L-methylfolate given some evidence in bipolar depression and possible interruption of folate pathway with valproate.
8/4/23: Ongoing depression, requesting an SSRI.

William B Seretta is a 36 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more

comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic
medications. Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin,
which is currently used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be
continued for the time being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider
initiation of alpha agonist medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating
mania/psychosis than stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and
physician will be crucial in providing effective care for the patient.

William B Seretta is a 36 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic
medications. Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin,
which is currently used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be
continued for the time being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider
initiation of alpha agonist medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating
mania/psychosis than stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and
physician will be crucial in providing effective care for the patient.
