William B Seretta is a 35 y.o. male with a history of bi
polar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime
hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic
medications. Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin,
which is currently used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be
continued for the time being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider
initiation of alpha agonist medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating
mania/psychosis than stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and
physician will be crucial in providing effective care for the patient.

William B Seretta is a 35 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic
medications. Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin,
which is currently used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be
continued for the time being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider
initiation of alpha agonist medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating
mania/psychosis than stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and
physician will be crucial in providing effective care for the patient.

William B Seretta is a 35 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who

presented as a referral from SHH after his first life
time hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic
medications. Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin,
which is currently used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be
continued for the time being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider
initiation of alpha agonist medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating
mania/psychosis than stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and
physician will be crucial in providing effective care for the patient.

William B Seretta is a 35 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis

of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic
medications. Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin,
which is currently used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be
continued for the time being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider
initiation of alpha agonist medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating
mania/psychosis than stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and
physician will be crucial in providing effective care for the patient.

William B Seretta is a 35 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I
, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime
hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic
medications. Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin,
which is currently used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be
continued for the time being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider
initiation of alpha agonist medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating
mania/psychosis than stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and
physician will be crucial in providing effective care for the patient.
5/23: Reporting ongoing fatigue/pain from chronic Lyme. Little energy and motivation. Re-initiated on Adderall by PCP. Reports

Chief Complaint: Neuropathy follow-up

**Polyneuropathy, peripheral sensorimotor axonal**
35-year-old man with B12 deficiency and was found to have a severe axonal generalized sensorimotor polyneuropathy on nerve
conduction testing 6 months ago. The etiology of his B12 deficiency is most likely related to an acute and high-dose exposure to
nitrous oxide prior to the development of the symptoms. This was unknown at his last visit. Nitrous oxide causes inactivation of the
B12 dependent enzyme methionine synthase. This occurs in a dose-dependent fashion. His high-dose exposure is the most likely
cause of his severe neuropathy. Thankfully with cessation of nitrous oxide use and B12 replacement his symptoms have improved
though he remains with persistent signs of a sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Some degree of permanent damage is certainly
possible.
– We discussed the likely etiology of his polyneuropathy.
– He is highly encouraged to continue to avoid nitrous oxide use.
– No further work-up is needed at this time.
– He may return here as needed.
HPI: 35-year-old man with a history of reactive arthritis and B12 deficiency who was seen 6 months ago for evaluation of lower
extremity numbness and tingling. He was found to have evidence of a severe generalized sensorimotor polyneuropathy.
Strength has been fine. He has noted that the tingling in his LE has receded a bit. This is now involving the feet to the mid shins. He
has normal sensation in his hands. He attributes his improvement to having his B12 levels normalized.
His balance has been alright. He has not had any falls.

William B Seretta is a 35 y.o. male
with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who presented as a referral from SHH after
his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.

On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's history of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing
sobriety is paramount to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial
evaluation, and is amenable to stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will
be necessary, with rapid referral to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic
medications. Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin,
which is currently used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be
continued for the time being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider
initiation of alpha agonist medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating
mania/psychosis than stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and
physician will be crucial in providing effective care for the patient.

**III. HPI **(include current psych ROS):
William B Seretta is a 34 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, cannabis use, nitrous oxide use, and gambling addiction who presents
after a referral from SHH after his first lifetime psychiatric hospitalization. Patient was hospitalized on an involuntary basis from
3/11-4/5 due to manic symptoms in the community eventually leading to an altercation with his father and subsequent police
involvement.
During his hospitalization, he was weaned off of his home medications of fluoxetine, lamotrigine, Adderall and clonazepam while
he was titrated onto Depakote and olanzapine. The olanzapine was cross-titrated to haloperidol due to weight gain towards the
latter part of the hospitalization. Patient was euthymic without signs of psychosis at time of discharge.
Of note, patient's mother contacted the family navigator at SHH reporting that the patient had once again become paranoia and
delusional. She was unsure if patient was still on his medications.
Today, the patient presents on time for his scheduled appointment. On interview, he presents with a bright affect and linear
thought process.
Patient reports that he suspects that he has struggled with bipolar for many years and notes that he has had several episodes of
bipolar. He notes that his most recent episode was the most severe which led to his hospitalization; notes that is family noticed that
things were much worse than he was able to notice. When we reviewed aspects of his presentation in the chart the patient did
agree with what was reported, though he does note that he did not feel as ill as his parents made him out to be. He additionally
reports some social strife with his parents due to the events that led to his hospitalization (reports that they told him he was going
to the ED for an intake not for hospitalization) and still reports that they are having interpersonal difficulties because they are not
trusting of him.
Patient reports that he is mood and psychotic symptoms have been largely in control with his current medication regimen.

He reports a history of repeated manic episodes, estimating they happen 1-2 times a year, with depression predominating the
remainder of his time. He notes that during his manic episodes he will spend money excessively, make irrational decisions, will
sleep a little during the night and more during the day, experience racing thoughts and grandiose delusions. He notes that these
instances last a couple of days. Often during these times, he will spend all the money that he has saved throughout the year.
Patient also reports a history of gambling addiction where he would engage in sports batting and subsequently blackjack which
she would play online. He notes that he has "played through $3 million." It is unclear whether his behaviors occurred in the context
of a manic episode or during periods of euthymia.
During his depressive periods, he states that he will be in bed all day, have little energy to go throughout the day, will feel
excessively guilty about things he has done and will not do certain things because he does not feel he "deserves it." He denies any
suicidal ideation during this time.
Currently, the patient states that he is struggling primarily with anxiety and with symptoms of ADHD. He reports ongoing
difficulties with inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability. He reports that he is going to be starting a job working in data analysis
that his family friend had gotten him and is worried about his ability to perform at this job. In regards to
his anxiety, he reports that he has a constant feeling of anxiety, which can increase at times and cause physical symptoms such as
tightness in chest and digestive issues. He reports that he spends most of his time worrying about finances, stating that his parents
had accidentally wiped a hard drive that he had with BitCoin on it, as well as his dad ripping up debit cards that were mailed to
him. He endorses feelings of poor concentration and fatigue related to his anxiety.

**XII. Evaluation Summary and Formulation***: *
William B Seretta is a 34 y.o. male with a history of bipolar I, ADHD, history of inhalant misuse (nitrous), and cannabis use who
presented as a referral from SHH after his first lifetime hospitalization due to manic and psychosis in the community.
On initial evaluation, the patient appears euthymic and without overt psychotic symptoms on the medication regimen of Depakote
and Haldol. He does report some historical elements which may represent grandiose delusions (e.g. having had several million
dollars, having millions of followers on Instagram, releasing highly successful music) though without collateral information this is
hard to fully ascertain. Will discuss with former outpatient psychiatrist, and should patient allow, discuss with parents for more
comprehensive history. Primary complaints on evaluation were symptoms of anxiety and inattention which have persisted despite
treatment of his underlying mood disorder. Differential for the symptoms include ADHD, combined type given history of
inattention, hyperactivity, and irritability; though this is confounded by patient's daily cannabis use. Could also consider diagnosis
of generalized anxiety disorder given symptoms of generalized worry, poor concentration and fatigue.
Given patient's h
istory of significant inhalant use with subsequent medical sequela (e.g. peripheral polyneuropathy), ongoing sobriety is paramount
to maintaining psychiatric stability. Fortunately, the patient endorses only using cannabis on initial evaluation, and is amenable to
stopping this in order to mitigate inattentive symptoms. Close monitoring of his substance use will be necessary, with rapid referral
to substance use treatment program should he relapse in his inhalant use.
Therapeutically, the patient appears to be benefiting with a combination of mood stabilizing and antipsychotic medications.
Patient's Haldol may require titration if delusional thought content becomes more apparent. Patient's gabapentin, which is currently
used for polyneuropathy, can also be increased in order to target his anxiety. As needed clonazepam will be continued for the time
being while more permanent treatment options for anxiety are developed. Additionally, can consider initiation of alpha agonist
medications for symptoms of inattention and anxiety, as these have much less chance of precipitating mania/psychosis than
stimulant medications. Finally, building a therapeutic alliance and maintaining trust between patient and physician will be crucial in
providing effective care for the patient.

**Summary of Clinical Course**
Summary: This was a first psychiatric hospitalization for this patient, targeting stabilization of mania and psychosis. Diagnostically,
their symptoms are consistent with a diagnosis of bipolar 1 disorder.
The patient was admitted to 2W in the usual fashion. While the patient initially presented with irritability, grandiosity, and tendency
to become easily agitated, there were no major behavioral issues during hospitalization, including no psychiatric emergencies,
seclusions, or restraints. A phone restriction was put in place after the patient repeatedly called 911 and several police departments
seeking aid in being discharged. Diagnostically, the patient's presentation was consistent with a first episode mania with psychosis.
The patient endorsed nitrous oxide use leading up to hospitalization, raising concern for a possible contribution of substances to
his presentation. His home medications were stopped in the ED, including fluoxetine, lamotrigine, Adderall, and clonazepam. He
was started on olanzapine and depakote. He demonstrated improvement in mood primarily with titration of depakote. Dose was
titrated to 2500 mg with a valproate level of 111. His CMP demonstrated slight elevations in LFTs, and while he remained
asymptomatic, dose was decreased to 2250 mg. Olanzapine was increased to a total daily dose of 40 mg, with persistent symptoms
of psychosis. In addition, the patient gained approximately 20 pounds during the first 2 weeks of hospitalization while taking
olanzapine. For these reasons, olanzapine was cross-titrated to haloperidol. The patient demonstrated euthymic mood with
resolution of delusional thinking and paranoia. He demonstrated insight into his substance use and expressed motivation for
sobriety.
The care team spoke with the patient's parents on several occassions. A family meeting took place prior to discharge. Parents
discussed expectations for the patient to return home, which were agreed upon.
This APP became involved in the patient's care on the day prior to and the day of discharge. At the time of discharge, the patient is
safe and forward thinking without any suicidal ideation whatsoever. He is eating well, sleeping well, and attending to ADLs. He is
showing no signs of mania or psychosis. He is agreeable to working collaboratively with the social worker and this provider on
discharge planning, signing documents, discussing aftercare and a safety plan. The patient's acute suicide risk is low at this time. He
denied SI for duration of hospitalization and has no history of suicide attempts. He is aware of crisis resources and completed a
safety plan prior to discharge.

William B Seretta is a 34 y.o. male with prior diagnoses of bipolar 2 disorder, anxiety, and ADHD who presents as an involuntary
patient from the MMC ED with symptoms of mania. Symptoms have reportedly been present for several weeks and the patient has
recently threatened violence towards family members and police. His parents have found several 100 empty whippit containers in
the patient's room, raising concern for a substance-induced component to his presentation. The patient has been adherent with
olanzapine and depakote in the emergency department, with some improvement noted, however he remains grandiose, irritable,
delusional, and has extremely poor insight.

manic and agitated. He could not tolerate interview with the care team and was yelling loudly before terminating the meeting. He
has called 911 repeatedly despite redirection from staff. Phone restriction will be put in place.

remains delusional with extremely poor insight. Weight g
ain noted and likely attributable to olanzapine. At this time, benefit of this medication outweighs ongoing risk of weight gain.
3/24: Given ongoing delusional/paranoid thinking and significant weight gain (~20lbs) with high dose olanzapine, plan to taper
and introduce haloperidol now that depakote is therapeutic.

3/31: Patient presents as euthymic with improvement in delusions. Engaged in successful family meeting discussing transition
home. We are establishing aftercare with plan for discharge home next week.

Summary: SHH Admission Nurse Note

This is a 34 yo SWM being referred by MMC-ED for Involuntary In-Pt. Treatment. He lives in Yarmouth with his parents. He has
Medicare and Mainecare. He is reportedly unemployed but references a job, "making music." This is his 1st In-Pt. Psychiatric
Admission. He has a PCP, addiction counselor, (for gambling,) and a Psychiatric provider. He is Rx. Medication. Per referral, Pt.
arrived at the ED on 3/7/2022 accompanied by his parents, with Hx. of Bipolar D/O, Anxiety and ADHD, with medical Dx including
Polyneuropathy and chronic Lyme disease. ED and family reported Pt. with mania over the past 2-3 weeks culminating in aggressive
behavior towards family and Police. He reported not taking his meds recently and he denied recent SA. Parents reported Pt. with
mania, grandiosity, paranoia, and spending increased amounts on Marijuana and "whippits." On Thursday, Pt. reportedly had a fight
with father over the use of the car and Pt. called the Police stating he was being choked, (although Police found no evidence of.)
Police encouraged him to sleep elsewhere and Pt. reportedly slept in his car, at friends and in a hotel. Pt. had reportedly made
threats to attack the Police with a knife if they were called on him, and attack others if he was taken to the hospital. While in ED, he
presented hyperactive, with mood lability, irritability, grandiose, perseverative, with rapid speech and flight of ideas, paranoia and
delusions. He reported his family sabotaging his ability to "succeed in life." He spoke of meeting with executives from a music
company, Apple and Google. He also spoke of large amounts of Crypto currency and need to "divest." At one point in ED, Pt.
wanted to leave and threatened "to fight my way out if I need to." He denied SIB, SI, HI, or AVH. Pt. currently reports he is being
admitted because his parent
s lied to get him here. They said he had threatened with a knife, and he denies any such threats. He states he is going to sue his
parents and he has a lawyer through Joe Bornstein." He presents as polite, cooperative, and pleasant in his interactions with staff.
He was cooperative with the interview and able to take direction from staff for search process. His affect was bright, smiling much
of the time. Eye contact was good, speech was clear. He tends to get ahead of the interview but was cooperative with redirection.
He states he is here and agreeable to working with the team. He continues to deny SIB, recent/current SI or plan/intent to harm/kill
self in community or SHH. He reports he will seek out staff and talk if feeling uncomfortable, upset or unsafe on Unit. He denies HI
and denies making threats to others. He denies recent abuse/trauma, although feels father has been verbally abusive his whole life.
He states he last used Alcohol 9/2021 when he had a couple Beers. He denies any issues with alcohol. He reports he vapes MJ/THC
and uses some edibles. He smokes a few hits a day, but was vague with amounts/frequency of edibles. He last used "Whippits,"
over a month ago, at that time was using a box of 50/day. He denies the use of any other substance recently. Pt. was safe during his
stay in admissions and was monitored on 1:1 status then changed to 15 minute checks by Attending, (Dr. Powers,) following report
by this writer. He complained of chronic BLE pain from the knees down from having frostbite previously. He rated the pain as a "4"
and described it as tingly and numb. He states he treats it with a lot of Ibuprofen at home. Report was given to 2 West Unit Nurse,
(Kim.) Pt. Was searched and escorted to Unit without reported incident.

Chief Complaint: Lower extremity numbness
**Polyneuropathy, peripheral sensorimotor axonal**
34-year-old man with a rheumatologic condition causing primarily lower extremity joint pains and swelling who has also been
diagnosed with B12 deficiency earlier this fall, already treated with B12 replacement. He has been experiencing numbness and
tingling primarily in the distal lower extremities over the last year. His examination demonstrates reduced muscle bulk in the distal
lower extremities. Vibratory sensation is markedly abnormal in the feet. His electrophysiologic testing demonstrated evidence of a
severe, axonal generalized sensorimotor polyneuropathy. His skin temperature was noted to be markedly reduced. It was difficult to
adequately warm his distal lower extremities. This could account for the mildly prolonged distal latencies and moderately slowed
conduction velocities. The etiology of his polyneuropathy is not clear. Some contribution from his significant B12 deficiency is
possible. It is also possible that this is related to his rheumatologic condition. His neuropathy is not consistent with an
inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy which could be seen in association with TNF inhibitors. Previous laboratory testing
has demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers, normal serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation. He does not have
any history of elevated blood sugars to account for this. A neuropathy this severe and someone this age could also be the result of
a recessive axonal hereditary sensorimotor polyneuropathy.
–I would like to touch base with his rheumatologist in order to get a better sense of what he is being treated for.
–He should be receiving ongoing vitamin B12 replacement. A repeat level should have been done to make sure that his vitamin B12
level is now well within normal limits. We will contact his primary care doctor's office to see if they have done this.
–I would like to reevaluate him in approximately 3 months. He will call here if he notes progressive lower extremity weakness.

problems with numbness and tingling in the lower extremities for about the last year. He reports a history consistent with him
having a Lhermitte sign which involves the pain radiating down the spine with neck flexion. This is typically associated with cervical
spine lesions. His examination also demonstrates evidence of a length dependent polyneuropathy with reduced vibratory sensation
in the toes and reduced temperature sensation in a stocking distribution. His work-up thus far has not demonstrated any
abnormalities which would account for these symptoms other than a vitamin B12 deficiency which is now being treated. It is
possible that his significant neuropathy could be the result of his vitamin B12 deficiency depending on how long he had a low
vitamin B12 level. I would not expect neuropathy related to vitamin B12 deficiency affecting the feet to improve too quickly.
–In order to investigate his reported pain down the spine with neck flexion I will obtain an MRI scan of the cervical spine.
–We also discussed the fact that autoimmune conditions can have neuropathy as an associated issue, both large fiber and small
fiber neuropathy.
–He will also return here for EMG and nerve conduction studies to further characterize his neuropathy.
HPI: 34-year-old man with a history of severe depression and an autoimmune form of arthritis who is referred for evaluation of
numbness and tingling. He is seen along with his mother.
He estimates that his current problem with numbness and tingling began in the last year. He has had pain in his joints for years
which is what lead to a diagnosis of reactive arthritis. He has been treated with Simponi for the last couple of years. He thinks
Simponi has had a mild benefit in terms of pain reduction. He has had less joint swelling on this medication.
His numbness and tingling began in his lower back. He states that he has had tingling in the low back for a long time. Tingling is
more prominent in the toes and is better up the legs. He reports that with neck flexion he has significant pain radiating down the
spine. He has had some numbness in the finger tips but states that this improved after starting treatment for B12 deficiency. He has
had 4 weekly injections of B12. His vitamin B12 level on September 14 was less than 150. His symptoms overall have improved
quite a bit with this treatment. He has been diagnosed with chronic lyme in the past. He reports that brain fog, memory issues,
ankle and knee swelling were symptoms from this. Treatment began 4-5 years ago. He is not receiving any treatment for this at the
current time. There was also a suspicion for mold toxicity. Other recent laboratory testing demonstrates an elevated CRP level at
9.5. TSH was normal. A CBC was normal. Sed rate was normal. Folate level was normal. Serum protein electrophoresis with
immunofixation was negative. A Lyme antibody screen was negative. He has had MRI scans of his lumbar spine and thoracic spine
which have not demonstrated any abnormalities to explain his symptoms.
He reports that his legs have been very weak.
Denies having any difficulties with bowel or bladder function.
He has not had any falls. His balance is off.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

Elizabeth, RN - 11/11/2020 7:55 AM EST

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

Elizabeth, RN - 10/21/2020 9:52 AM EDT
Formatting of this note is different from the original.
ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

Elizabeth, RN - 10/07/2020 8:14 AM EDT

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.
** You are due for a required annual physical exam with your PCP by October 21, 2020, along with a CBC and BMP. Please make
sure to schedule this with your doctor so as not to interrupt your ECT schedule.
** Talk with Dr. Abernathy about partial hospital and whether she feels this or a therapist may be helpful moving forward.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.
*** You are due for an annual physical exam along with CBC and CMP before October 21, 2020.

Discharge Instructions
Elizabeth, RN - 08/12/2020 8:27 AM EDT
Formatting of this note is different from the original.
ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

Elizabeth, RN - 07/14/2020 11:27 AM EDT

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

impaired.

procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

Elizabeth, RN - 04/03/2020 7:14 AM EDT

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Have you been in close proximity with someone who is currently sick with the COVID-19 or any other respiratory illness within the
past 14 days? Do they have a fever, a new cough in the last 14 days, shortness of breath, a sore throat or a runny nose? If so, please
call the ECT coordinator before coming in for your appointment.
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.

ECT DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
• After your treatment you may feel drowsy and have a problem concentrating.
• Stay at home and rest for the remainder of the day.
• No driving at all during an acute or index ECT series (two or more treatments per week). Cognition and concentration may be
impaired.
• Once in the maintenance/continuation phase of ECT (no more than one treatment per week), do not drive for 24 hours after your
procedure.
• Be cautious about making major decisions while you are undergoing ECT.
• Eat small meals often at first and increase slowly.
• Call the ECT coordinator by dialing 662-3129 for any problems you feel are related to your procedure, or go to the nearest
emergency room.
FOR YOUR NEXT ECT APPOINTMENT:
• Do not have anything to eat or drink after midnight the night prior to your treatment. If you have a later appointment and need
fluids, you may have clear liquids (water, gatorade, apple juice, cranberry juice) up until two hours prior to hour appointment time.
• If you are on a benzodiazepine or anti-seizure medication, do not take this medication after 6P the night prior to your treatment.
• The morning of your treatment, do not take your morning medications unless instructed to do so.
• You should take your scheduled morning cardiac medications and medications for indigestion with a small sip of water two (2)
hours prior to your appointment.
• Remove all head and neck jewelry before coming in for your treatment.
• Keep hair free of all hair products other than shampoo and conditioner.
• Make sure you have arranged for someone to drive you home and that you have someone who can stay with you if needed if you
are confused.
• If you have any questions prior to your scheduled treatment, please call Beth Perry, RN, ECT Coordinator, at 662-3129.
*** Please complete QIDS SR16 on Thursday and bring it with you to your next appointment.

Elizabeth, RN - 03/04/2020 10:46 AM EST
